paras: The lynching of Tom Gordon was the hanging of a man accused of killing the city marshal of Socorro, New Mexico Territory, by a mob at Socorro in March 1881. Gordon had escaped to Albuquerque, was rearrested there and taken back to Socorro, where a mob numbered in the hundreds hanged him to a water tank. The story reached eastern and southern papers through a single Kansas City dispatch, reprinted widely in mid-March.

According to the Kansas City dispatch, Gordon, described as "a desperado," killed the city marshal of Socorro "a few days ago" and then escaped and fled to Albuquerque. No report names the marshal, describes the killing or gives Gordon's race.

Gordon was rearrested at Albuquerque and taken back to Socorro, the scene of the marshal's killing. The dispatches date this to "Friday last," which before datelines of March 15 to 17 fell on March 11, 1881, though some versions attach the day to the arrest and others to the return to Socorro. At Socorro, a Wilmington paper said, he "was seized by a mob and lynched."

The fuller versions say the mob hanged him to a water tank, a public site in the town rather than a remote one. None of the reports gives the time of day or describes onlookers apart from the mob itself.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the mob, or other official response was found in the coverage.

White papers from Maine to Texas printed the item between March 16 and 18, nearly always as a Kansas City special relayed by way of St. Louis and credited in some versions to the St. Louis Republican. Headlines named Gordon by his alleged crime or reputation, among them "Murderer Lynched" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, "Hanged by a Mob" in the Wheeling Register and "A Desperado's Fate" in the Delaware State Journal. The Savannah Morning News ran "LYNCHING IN NEW MEXICO. The Desperado Who Killed the City Marshal Hanged in Socorro," and the Memphis Daily Appeal printed the item under a heading that reads in the scan as "Thinning Out the Desperadoes."

Shorter forms appeared in news briefs, including the Lancaster Intelligencer's "Lynching in New Mexico" under "Violent Deaths," which gave no method or crowd size. A week later weekly papers in New Jersey and Rhode Island carried a condensed version in their crime and news digests, saying he was hanged "by a crowd of 200 or 300 men." No paper questioned Gordon's guilt or commented on the mob's action; the papers treated the killing of the marshal as fact.

The size of the mob varies across printings of the same dispatch: 300 men in the two Wheeling papers, two or three hundred in most others, and "five or seven hundred" in the Dallas Daily Herald. Because all versions descend from one Kansas City special, the most widely printed figure of 200 or 300 is likely closest to the original text.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Gordon
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Every report says Gordon, accused of killing the Socorro city marshal, was hanged or lynched by a mob after being brought back to Socorro under arrest (A3, A7, A8).

A mob of two or three hundred or more hanged Gordon to a water tank without any legal proceeding, in retaliation for the killing of the city marshal of which he was accused (A3, A8, A12); his race is not stated in any report.
Every article traces to one Kansas City special relayed through St. Louis (A2, A3, A8); no local New Mexico report, inquest or later follow-up was found, though the versions agree on the core event.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Kansas City special nearly verbatim under headlines such as 'Murderer Lynched', 'Hanged by a Mob' and 'A Desperado's Fate', treating Gordon's guilt as settled.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'LYNCHING IN NEW MEXICO. The Desperado Who Killed the City Marshal Hanged in Socorro.', with no editorial comment.
Weekly digests folded the item into crime roundups ('Record of Crime') among other killings and hangings.

On or shortly after March 11; 'Friday last' refers to the arrest in some versions.
